A TFSA investment loss changes your wealth, not your unused contribution room

Use four graphics to separate investment value, cash withdrawn and the ordinary withdrawal amount added back as room in the next calendar year.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate a hypothetical TFSA value change from its room record

Original hypothetical nominal-CAD TFSA illustration using the ordinary-room framework in the cited CRA guidance, reviewed 25 October 2026. The opening contribution is assumed lawful and already completed; the separately entered unused room is the reconciled amount remaining across all the holder’s TFSAs afterward. The holder is assumed eligible and resident in Canada throughout the illustrated sequence. One investment-value change is followed by one ordinary withdrawal; proceeds remain as outside cash with no spending or further return. The investment-value change alters account value but not unused contribution room. The ordinary withdrawal’s amount is added back on 1 January of the next calendar year, not immediately. The next-year room chart is only carried unused room plus this withdrawal’s addback: it deliberately excludes the new annual dollar limit and every other transaction or adjustment, so it is not a full next-year room calculation. No actual contribution request, excess tax, fee, direct transfer, specified distribution, non-resident period, non-qualified investment or personal eligibility determination is modeled.

The central idea

A loss inside a TFSA is not a withdrawal. A later ordinary withdrawal adds back the amount actually withdrawn next year, rather than automatically restoring the original contribution.

01

Keep value, cash movements and contribution room in separate records

A TFSA can have one account value and a different amount of unused contribution room. An investment loss changes the value of what is held. A withdrawal moves money out. The room record follows the applicable contribution and withdrawal rules, rather than simply mirroring the account balance.

CRA’s contribution guidance states that investment-value changes do not affect TFSA contribution room and that an investment loss does not count as a withdrawal. The loss itself is not added back as room.

The tool begins just after one assumed lawful contribution. Its unused-room input is already reconciled across the holder’s TFSAs after that contribution. It does not establish eligibility or reconstruct anyone’s full contribution history.

02

Follow the investment change before making any withdrawal

The default opening contribution is CAD 10,000, assumed permitted using previously available room. A 20% investment decline reduces the account value by CAD 2,000 to CAD 8,000. No money has been withdrawn at this stage.

The room amount entered after the opening contribution remains unchanged. With the default of zero unused room, the loss does not create a new CAD 2,000 deposit allowance. Replacing the lost value with new money would require room available for that contribution through the applicable record.

The waterfall shows only the value arithmetic: CAD 10,000 minus CAD 2,000 equals CAD 8,000. It does not record the loss as a cash payment to the holder or a transaction that restores contribution capacity.

03

Use the amount actually withdrawn for the next-year addback

The default then withdraws 100% of the remaining CAD 8,000 as an ordinary withdrawal. Account value falls to zero and CAD 8,000 becomes cash held outside the TFSA. Under the reviewed ordinary-withdrawal framework, that CAD 8,000 is the amount added back as room on the next 1 January.

CRA’s withdrawal guidance explains that an ordinary withdrawal does not create new room immediately. Re-contributing during the same calendar year requires sufficient unused room already available. The related calendar guide examines that timing constraint in more detail.

The withdrawal-based addback in this example is CAD 2,000 below the original CAD 10,000 contribution. That comparison concerns this selected withdrawal only. It is not a complete next-year contribution limit, a required deposit or an estimate of how much the investment could later recover.

04

Room returning does not restore money lost

The stacked bars track financial resources separately from the room bars. Before the withdrawal, CAD 8,000 is inside the account. Afterward, CAD 8,000 is outside as retained cash. The total is unchanged by the withdrawal because the model assumes no fees or spending.

On the next 1 January, the ordinary withdrawal affects the room record, but there is still only CAD 8,000 of financial resources in this illustration. Adding the room amount to the cash amount as though both were assets would count permission to contribute as money.

Rebuilding wealth requires investment changes or additional saving. The model does not project a recovery or recommend keeping, selling or replacing an investment. Its purpose is to keep the value and room calculations from being confused.

05

Test partial withdrawals and gains without changing the rule

Change the withdrawal share to 50% while keeping the default 20% decline. The ordinary withdrawal is then CAD 4,000, with CAD 4,000 still in the TFSA. The withdrawal-based next-year addback is CAD 4,000, not the whole remaining account value and not the original contribution.

Now try a 20% investment gain and a full ordinary withdrawal. The account reaches CAD 12,000, and the assumed withdrawal is CAD 12,000. The gain alone did not change room while it remained invested; the amount actually withdrawn is what enters this ordinary-withdrawal addback illustration.

The matrix combines several value changes and withdrawal shares. Every cell holds the original contribution fixed and calculates the assumed withdrawal after the selected move. It contains neither a future annual dollar limit nor probabilities for market outcomes.

06

Complete the room calculation with the actual record before contributing

The room chart deliberately excludes the new calendar year’s annual dollar limit. It also excludes other contributions, withdrawals, transfers and adjustments. Its final bar is only a subtotal of carried unused room plus this one ordinary withdrawal.

For example, entering CAD 3,000 of unused room after the original contribution would leave that amount unchanged by the market decline and the same-year withdrawal. Adding the default CAD 8,000 ordinary withdrawal next year produces a CAD 11,000 subtotal before the omitted annual limit and any other adjustments.

CRA recommends reconciling contribution room using the holder’s own records. The model assumes Canadian residency and eligibility throughout, and it excludes specified distributions, transfer treatment, excess histories and other special situations. Use the applicable full record rather than an account value or this partial illustration before making a real contribution.
